transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-22 14:00 PT | Duration: 75 mins
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Samir Gupta (Redwood SE); Jordan Lee (Sparrow Head of ML), Priya Nair (Infra), Devon Price (Product), Anita Zhao (Security)

[00:00:00] Lena: Alright everyone, thanks for carving out the time. The goal today is to land on a reproducible benchmark methodology so both teams can compare latency/throughput across hosted, dedicated and an on-prem VPC test. We'll go through prompts, load patterns, caching semantics and quantizeation experiments.
[00:00:23] Jordan: Great, we've been waiting for this. Our priorities are clear — tail latency p99 needs to be < 350ms for the checkout micro-copy flow, cost targets are softer but we'd like to quantify them. Also we care about data residency — the proof will likely be on-prem.
[00:00:38] Marco: Cool. Quick note: when we say p99 we want a consistent measurement window and warmup protocol. Cold starts and queueing can skew numbers. We'll propose a 15 minute warmup with prefix cache state populated, then run a 30 minute steady-state plus a few burst scenarios.
[00:00:58] Priya: Question — how do you handle the K V cache on dedicated vs hosted? We saw different behaviors in the initial PoC where the session cache didn't persist across quick scale events.
[00:01:12] Marco: Right, good callout. There's subtlety: our runtime has a per-worker KV (we often call it K V cache in logs) and a prefix cache layer. For apples-to-apples we need to define whether the benchmark includes prefix-hits or measures cold prefix misses. We'll include both: 1) cold from empty cache, 2) warmed prefix-only, 3) warmed KV cache with chat history.
[00:01:37] Devon: That makes sense. For our use case most users only see short chat context — 256 tokens — but checkout flows have longer prompts up to 800 tokens when we attach product context.
[00:01:50] Samir: Noted. We'll include two prompt families: a short 200-token transactional set and a long 800-token context-enriched set. Also we'll publish tokenization details since token counts vary by tokenizer.
[00:02:07] Lena: We should also align on quantization. Sparrow mentioned accuracy sensitivity; Marco, can you walk through the plan?
[00:02:14] Marco: Sure. Proposal: compare FP16 baseline, 8-bit post-training quant profiles and a 4-bit LLM-int8-style config if you want aggressive cost savings. We'll run Nucleus-sampling and greedy inferences and measure exact-match and semantic-similarity on a held-out evaluation set from your product prompts. There will be minor noise — e.g., quanta zation artifacts — so we recommend repeating runs three times and reporting median + IQR.
[00:02:45] Jordan: How do you ensure the models themselves are comparable? We don't want a situation where a smaller model with heavier quant gives better throughput but far worse quality.
[00:02:55] Marco: Good point — we'll define model variant pairs: same architecture and checkpoint where the only change is quant profile, or if that's not possible we'll pick the nearest family and call out differences. We'll provide a model selection rationale doc.
[00:03:08] Anita: On security — we need to see SOC2 Type II reports, KMS integration details, and whether HSM-backed key wraps are supported. Also clarify what logs include PII so we can redact.
[00:03:20] Lena: We'll share security artifacts. For the on-prem test, Redwood Private can be deployed with customer-managed KMS and audit logs forwarded to your SIEM. We'll attach the security pack after the call.
[00:03:33] Anita: Awesome, please include sample audit log entries — we had trouble mapping fields in the trial.
[00:03:39] Marco: We'll add a log mapping table. Back to load — Priya, what does your baseline traffic look like? Are there diurnal spikes or sudden bursts?
[00:03:49] Priya: We have steady traffic but big spikes during promotions — up to 12x baseline for short windows. Also we have a strict egress limit to certain regions; if the on-prem lab can't egress to Redwood-hosted endpoints we'll need to run the agent locally and collect telemetry.
[00:04:05] Lena: For the lab, we can run a private connector and an on-prem agent that writes metrics to a local collector, then upload aggregates. That avoids egress of user data.
[00:04:15] Jordan: What's the proposed load generator setup? We need to replicate user think-time and distribution of prompt lengths.
[00:04:22] Samir: We recommend a replay-driven generator. We'll give you a capture spec and a small harness that can replay based on time-of-day distributions, ramp patterns and user think-time. Key is to reproduce arrival process (Poisson vs bursty). For the apples-to-apples comparo we'll use the same seeds across all runs.
[00:04:40] Devon: How do you handle streaming responses in the benchmark? Our client is tuned for streaming to reduce perceived latency.
[00:04:47] Marco: We'll provide both end-to-end total-latency (time-to-first-token and time-to-final-token) and streaming throughput metrics. For streaming we capture TTF (time-to-first) plus token-rate after first token. We'll also measure p50/p95/p99 on TTF and tail of time-to-final.
[00:05:05] Jordan: Are you capturing GPU utilization and per-request compute cost? We want to translate that to $/1000 requests.
[00:05:11] Marco: Yes — the runbook includes CPU/GPU metrics, memory, and scheduler queue lengths. We'll produce a unit-cost model (tokens/sec, GPU-hours) so you can compare across configs. We'll also note that batching changes token accounting — effective throughput vs latency tradeoff.
[00:05:29] Priya: About batching: do you support continuous batching or only fixed batch windows? We saw time-based batching that increased p99 unexpectedly in prior tests.
[00:05:38] Samir: The runtime supports continuous batching with adaptive time-slicing. In the benchmark we'll test three modes: no batching (single-request), small-time-window batching (e.g. 10ms/20ms), and continuous-batching tuned for throughput. We'll log the batching window distribution for each run so you can see headroom.
[00:05:56] Anita: For on-prem, will the autoscaler behave the same as hosted? Scaling in local k8s may differ and cause transient cache loss.
[00:06:05] Marco: Correct — we will capture scale-up/scale-down events and correlate with tail latency blips. For apples-to-apples, when comparing hosted vs private, we will either disable autoscale or configure identical scale policies and snapshot the node counts during the run.
[00:06:20] Lena: Quick formatting note: we'll produce a benchmark spreadsheet with tabs: prompts, load-config, warmup protocol, metric-definitions, model-variants, run-results. That will be the single source of truth.
[00:06:33] Jordan: Sounds good. A silly question: do you include tokenizer differences? We had differences in token counts between model forks and that changed throughput numbers.
[00:06:42] Marco: Yes — we standardize tokenizers and include a token mapping step. We'll include raw text, tokenized counts, and tokenization library versions.
[00:06:49] Devon: For accuracy metrics you mentioned semantic-similarity. Can you be specific? We want reproducible metrics not just hand-wavy evaluations.
[00:06:56] Marco: We'll compute embedding cosine similarity between baseline FP16 outputs and quantized outputs, plus BLEU and ROUGE where appropriate and a human-rated quality sample on 200 examples. We'll keep the eval set frozen across runs.
[00:07:07] Priya: Network setup for on-prem test: we can open a peering window May 29 between 02:00-08:00 UTC. Is that enough?
[00:07:16] Lena: Yes that's good. We'll schedule a 4-hour window for a full run and fallback shorter runs as needed.
[00:07:22] Anita: On logging PII — can you provide a redaction filter?
[00:07:27] Samir: We can run the harness with a redaction filter that replaces common PII patterns before exporting. We'll document what fields remain in logs.
[00:07:34] Jordan: Let's talk success criteria: 350ms p99 for short prompts, 900ms p99 for long prompts, and accuracy degradation < 3% for quantized 8-bit. These are starting points.
[00:07:46] Marco: We'll test to those thresholds and produce a tradeoff curve. If 8-bit fails accuracy, we'll recommend 4-bit only in non-critical flows.
[00:07:55] Lena: Ok concluding recap: share benchmark spreadsheet, runbook, security artifacts. Priya to confirm peering window, Marco to prep quant checklist, Anita to email compliance must-haves. We'll aim to run the on-prem experiment in the May 29 window.
[00:08:10] Jordan: Thanks all — that aligns with our expectations.
[00:08:13] Devon: Quick micro-question — will you provide the harness repo?
[00:08:17] Lena: Yes, Git repo link to the harness and a readme.
[00:08:20] Anita: Please ensure legal redlines are flagged before we share any data.
[00:08:25] Marco: Understood.
[00:08:30] (crosstalk)
[00:08:35] Lena: Alright we will follow up with calendar invites for the May 29 run and send the artifacts. Thanks everyone.
[00:08:41] End of recording
